Three comments:
- that argument, "engine = R" does not exist for function multinomPois
- have you tried to supply initial values ? Try to choose them as a good guess of where the solutions might be
- Have you tried a model with intercepts only ? Often, starting with the simplest model and then using solutions from one as initial values for the next-more-complex model is a good strategy

Regards  ---  Marc

messages.subject: pcountOpen: Hessian is not invertible
messages.subject_clean: pcountOpen: Hessian is not invertible
messages.body_plain:
I'm using pcountOpen for analysis of annual fish counts at 10 sites on a river with up to 6 spatial replicates (usually 3) per site for 16 years.  When I add any one of ten seasonal stream flow variables as a yearly site covariate on gamma, I get the error "Hessian is not invertible. Try using fewer covariates or providing starting values." I've tried using starting values but it doesn't help.  I've tried the same model with two species: one rare with low p (0.07) and one common with higher p (0.36).

The covariates I'd like to include to test for an effect on gamma are actually yearly covariates (i.e., they are the same for all sites within each year).  They represent seasonal flow patterns for the period between each annual survey.

When I created fake covariate data that varied across sites within each year, the same model ran without the error.

I'm not clear why one shouldn't be able to include yearly covariates on gamma (or omega) with the Dail-Madsen model.  Am I doing something silly?

hi Shane,
 if you sampled until 100 snakes were obtained then the likelihood for any model in unmarked is wrong.  The likelihood would have to be formulated conditional on n=100 which, in general, will depend on the encounter probability parameters of the model and the true local population size.
 I don't see an obvious easy fix to this from where you're at.
 Now , that said, I don't understand the variability in your observed sample sizes. So you sampled until n=100 or until some number of samples were made?

 In general the removal model should be appropriate for this type of removal data no matter how big the sample sizes are. However I think the stopping rule for sampling is important here.

regards
andy

messages.body_plain:
Andy, I hope you don't mind if I chase this down a bit...

I think I may have given you a mistaken impression of our sampling scheme and used 'observation' ambiguously.

All sampling "occasions" (Js, in your RxJ matrix) were conducted similarly, and during each "J" the majority of counts ("y"s) were only 0-3 snakes.  So, our desired sample of 100 snakes per site (R) dictated only how many Js we conducted at each R.  The way I see it, each occasion (J) yielded a count (y) that was drawn as a Poisson process from a site (R) with a true but unknown N (abundance).  My assumption is that the more Js we have for any R, the more "defined" the latent distribution, conditioned on N, becomes.  Hence, equality of number of sampling occasions (Js) should not be important...just that those sites with more sampling occasions should contain more information in the likelihood.

I believe I've heard the advice before that optimal study design would dedicate more effort (more Js) toward areas with lower abundance and/or detectability, and in a sense that is what happened by our continuing to collect 'y's of 0-3 per J, sometimes 3 or 4, until we've repeated enough Js for a sum of 100 per R, with each J being nearly identical in its level of effort.

I agree that if, on any given occasion (J) we called it a night when some number of snakes were captured, that would be a totally different beast, but in our case, each occasion was standardized and every snake found was collected, with no stopping rule other than the time limit on our search protocols.

With this clarification, do you still think pcount or multinomPois are inappropriate with the unbalanced sampling occasions due to lower counts at some sites?

Thanks,
Shane

messages.body_plain:
Hi, all.  I'm looking for guidance on how to account for variation in search effort (duration of search) among sampling occasions in a single-season (closed) pcount survey.

On each search occasion, an observer searches for snakes for a variable amount of time (dictated by logistical constraints, including weather, NOT by capture rates), with most non-urban habitat searches ( forest & savanna, 15 sites) being 100 to 180 minutes long and most urban searches (3 sites) being 45 to 120 minutes in duration.

What is the proper method for accounting for this variation in observation duration?  Some candidates:

minutes  <-pcount(~min ~site, data=umf)           #Duration as obsCov

intercept<-pcount(~min+h3 ~site, data=umf)        #Different intercepts by habitat

interact <-pcount(~min*h3 ~site, data=umf)        #Diff. slope/int by habitat

offset   <-pcount(~1+offset(min) ~site, data=umf) #Duration as offset

                       nPars     AIC   delta    AICwt cumltvWt

interact (min*habitat)    24 3831.55    0.00  1.0e+00     1.00

intercept(min+habitat)    22 3854.97   23.42  8.2e-06     1.00

minutes  (min)            20 3857.27   25.72  2.6e-06     1.00

offset   (offset(min))    19 4885.42 1053.87 1.4e-229     1.00

Allowing a different slope and intercept for each habitat type “fits” better, by far…but is this appropriate?  Does this allow the 1180 observations to explain an inordinate amount of the variation in encounter rates as opposed to abundance covariates at just 18 sites, or are observation and abundance so decoupled that this should not matter?

I’ve seen discussion in previous unmarked posts of including an "offset" term in the GLM formula as a constraint on the relationship (more time = higher counts, e.g. “exposure time”, more area = higher counts), but I’ll confess to not fully understanding how this works, including whether it should be offset(min) or offset(log(min)).  Further, including duration as an offset is nowhere in the ballpark with respect to AIC values.  Are models with an offset and without comparable in an AIC framework?

Thanks in advance.

--
Shane Siers

re. your questions in this mail, let me make a stab at a couple of answers. Most important perhaps, there is usually not a single proper way of doing things in modeling and modeling has elements of both a science and of an art (to paraphrase McCullagh & Nelder). So, in modeling as in real life, one should try not to get lost among a multitude of options.

In your case, all four candidates make sense to me (at least "looking from afar"), with the exception of the model with the offset: the offset argument should normally contain the natural log of the variable with which you want to "standardise" your counts (converting the counts to a "density" with respect to one unit of the offset). Then, if you let AIC play the role of a referee, the verdict is clearly in favour of one model. Now, if this model passes a goodness of fit test (e.g., using the parametric bootstrap) and yields estimates that make sense from what you know about the system, then I would go with this model. Except you or a knowledgable colleague comes up with a model that makes more sense based on a priori thinking about the biological system and the way in which your data were collected.

Kind regards  --  Marc

The offset function in R simply sets a model coefficient to 1, preventing the model from spending a parameter to estimate a beta coefficient for the given offset covariate.  Like Marc said, typically an offset is used to account for differences in sampling area or time to convert a count into a density or a rate, this while still making use of the Poisson distribution for the observed counts.  Since a Poisson regression models the linear predictor of the expected count on the log scale (i.e., the log link), the offset also needs to be on the log scale:

log(E[y/offset]) = lambda
log(E[y]) = log(offset) + lambda

So in your situation, by putting an offset in the observation model of pcount you are stating that capture probability scales linearly (on the logit scale) at a rate of 1.0 with the time spent searching.  Seems like a pretty restrictive assumption.  But otherwise yes, an offset term should be comparable in a model selection framework.

Hi all,

I would *not* use an offset for the detection part of the model. An offset is used if the expected count has a known relationship with one of the covariates. This would for instance be the case if Shane's sites differ in their area (I forgot whether they do, but this is important). Then, the expected abundance N(i) at a site i would be A(i) * lambda(i), you would specify log(A(i)) as an offset in your Poisson GLM or, equivalently, in the abundance part of your mixture model. lambda(i) would then be interpreted as the density per unit of A.

However, the searching time spent does not seem to have such a relationship to the expected observed count. That is, it is not reasonable to assume that 10 mins search time will produce twice as many snakes as 5 mins. Rather, I would estimate the relationship between the search time and the numbers of snakes caught and this is what you do if you treat "minutes" as a simple covariate (not as an offset). And this is the model that AIC says is the best.

Alternatively, perhaps your "sites" are not well-defined (say, they aren't all 1ha) and search time is a proxy for the area searched. Then, you could use search time in the model for abundance. The expected abundance would then scale to search time because a longer search would mean a larger area searched, but probably not linearly. One way how search time (or similar, route length) could be incorporated in a hierarchical model as a proxy for the area searched is sketched out in the paper by Royle and Dorazio in JABES (2006). They describe a three-level HM for M, N and the observed counts. M(i) is the population size at a site that is incompletely covered by sampling, so that the "exposed population size" is N(i), with N(i) <= M(i). You can treat N(i) ~ Binomial(M(i), theta), with theta being a function of route length. This model can be collapsed to a two-level model that can be fitted in unmarked by using 1/route length or 1/sampling effort as a covariate on abundance. See the attachment for a description by written by Andy Royle and Richard Chandler in their webinar on HMs.

So if people have searched increasingly larger areas at what is considered a "site" in Shane's study, then perhaps the reciprocal of search time could be incorporated as a covariate in the model for abundance.

Kind regards  --  Marc

I do not disagree with Marc's specific advice, but we argued earlier this year that it *is* appropriate to include an offset-like adjustment in detection models (Efford, Borchers & Mowat 2013 MEE 4:629; see 'General comments' in Discussion), in preference to a covariate. The user must take responsibility for assuming a constant detection rate per unit time is a reasonable model, but the cumulative hazard scale takes care of Marc's worry that 10 min != 2 x 5 min.
Murray

Shane

Dear Murray,

thanks for that suggestion. I haven't yet had the time to read your paper, but please let me ask you a question. I just talked with somebody who was using an N-mixture model for estimation of abundance based on data that had observation occasions that differed in length (e.g., between 1 and 10 min, from what I understood). What would you suggest is the best way to "standardise" detection probability for this unequal effort ?

I do not disagree with Marc's specific advice, but we argued earlier this year that it *is* appropriate to include an offset-like adjustment in detection models (Efford, Borchers & Mowat 2013 MEE 4:629; see 'General comments' in Discussion), in preference to a covariate. The appropriate adjustment is 'offset-like' because it is linear on a cumulative hazard scale, not the arbitrary link scale (one reason a simple covariate is *less* appropriate). This is a powerful and general tool, but as far as I know there is no implementation in non-spatial software. The user must take responsibility for assuming a constant detection rate per unit time is a reasonable model, but the cumulative hazard scale takes care of Marc's worry that 10 min != 2 x 5 min.
Murray

Hi all,

I would *not* use an offset for the detection part of the model. An offset is used if the expected count has a known relationship with one of the covariates. This would for instance be the case if Shane's sites differ in their area (I forgot whether they do, but this is important). Then, the expected abundance N(i) at a site i would be A(i) * lambda(i), you would specify log(A(i)) as an offset in your Poisson GLM or, equivalently, in the abundance part of your mixture model. lambda(i) would then be interpreted as the density per unit of A.

However, the searching time spent does not seem to have such a relationship to the expected observed count. That is, it is not reasonable to assume that 10 mins search time will produce twice as many snakes as 5 mins. Rather, I would estimate the relationship between the search time and the numbers of snakes caught and this is what you do if you treat "minutes" as a simple covariate (not as an offset). And this is the model that AIC says is the best.

Alternatively, perhaps your "sites" are not well-defined (say, they aren't all 1ha) and search time is a proxy for the area searched. Then, you could use search time in the model for abundance. The expected abundance would then scale to search time because a longer search would mean a larger area searched, but probably not linearly. Hi Marc

The idea is to think in terms of cumulative hazard of detection (lambda) rather than p (where lambda = -log(1-p) and p = 1 - exp(-lambda)). Other things being equal (!), lambda increases linearly with duration (effort). For any observed count there is a known duration ts; we parameterize in terms of the hazard lambda0 for a reference duration t0, so the detection probability for duration ts is 1 - exp(-ts/t0 * lambda0). This fits into the likelihood for a Poisson N-mixture model with R replicate populations sampled T times as follows:

neglogLik <- function (beta, n, ts, t0 = 1, maxN = 100) {
    ## beta is parameter vector (lambda0, N-bar) on log scale
    ## both n and ts should be matrices with dim (R,T)
    lambda0 <- exp(beta[1]);  N <- exp(beta[2])
    pt <- 1 - exp(-ts/t0 * lambda0)
    tmp <- sapply(0:maxN, dbinom, x = n, prob = pt)
    dim(tmp) <- c(nrow(n), ncol(n), maxN+1)
    tmp <- apply(tmp, c(1,3), prod)
    tmp <- sweep(tmp, MAR = 2, FUN ='*', STATS = dpois(0:maxN, N))
    -sum(log(apply(tmp,1,sum)))
}

I don't know if this can be done in unmarked.
Murray

Similar to Marc, I had plotted some figures to see how the cumulative hazard function for survey length compared to some logit-scale models for detection.  The code below shows how an offset for log(time) (beta coefficient = 1) and an estimated coefficient for log(time) (here I plotted beta = 2) compares to the cumulative hazard.  The plots are across different values of detection probability for the minimum survey length (p0).  Obviously the benefit of Murray's approach is that you do not have to estimate a separate parameter for the slope of the relationship, similar to an offset.

# mininum survey
t0<-1
# survey lengths
ts<-t0:10

for(p0 in round(10^(seq(-1,-.1,by=.1)),2)){
  lambda0 <- -1*log(1-p0)
  # detection over survey length
  pt <- 1-(exp(-ts/t0*lambda0))
  plot(ts,pt,type="l",xlim=c(0,10),ylim=c(0,1),main=paste("p0 =", p0),
     ylab="Detection probability",xlab="Survey length",las=1)
  lines(ts,plogis(qlogis(p0) + 1.0*log(ts)),col="blue")
  lines(ts,plogis(qlogis(p0) + 2.0*log(ts)),col="red")
  legend(6,.3,c("Hazard","1*log(time) [offset]","2*log(time)"),
         col=c("black","blue","red"),lty=1)
  browser()
}

pred=predict(bare,type="state",newdata=DF,backTran=FALSE,appendData=FALSE)
abun=exp(pred$Predicted)

av=mean(data$BARE)
stdv=sd(data$BARE)
xval=data.frame(BARE=seq(-0.5,5,0.5)*stdv+av)
matrix(data=c(LCL,abun,UCL),ncol=3,dimnames=list(xval$BARE))

final.SE<-predictSE.zip(final, se.fit=TRUE, parm.type="lambda",

messages.body_plain:
Hi Alejandro,

Both predict( ) in unmarked and predictSE.zip( ) in package AICcmodavg (>= version 1.35) produce the same prediction when using an offset. To illustrate what an offset does, you might want to experiment a bit with a Poisson distribution (instead of a ZIP).

When you are modelling an abundance as a rate (abundance per transect length for example), you are actually doing the following:

log(mu/transect.length) = linear predictor

log(mu) - log(transect.length) = linear predictor

log(mu) = linear predictor + log(transect.length)

Note that the linear predictor is the combination of beta estimates and explanatory variables forming the predictive equation.

Thus, if you want the predicted value of abundance for a given transect length, you have to exponentiate:

mu = exp(linear predictor + log(transect.length))

This is what happens with predict( ) and predictSE.zip( ) for a Poisson. For the zero-inflated Poisson, you must compute the linear predictor for the Poisson as above, but the final step involves:

mu = exp(linear predictor + log(transect.length)) * (1 - (exp(psi.pred)/(1 + exp(psi.pred))))

This is because the zero-inflated Poisson includes an additional parameter psi and its beta estimate is on a logit scale.

I suggest you work one of your examples using a simple model with only a single variable on abundance.

Hope it helps,

Marc M

messages.body_plain:
If you know how to use the reshape package to melt and cast your data frame, create a new column called "sampled" and set that to 1 for each record.  Then use melt and cast to create a matrix where the measured variable (measure.var) = "sampled" and set all zeros to NA.  Now when you create a matrix of the counts, you multiply it by the "sampled" matrix (which should be 1s and NAs).

data$sampled <- 1
data.melt1 <- melt(data, id.var=c("site","survey"), measure.var="sampled")
sample.matrix <- cast(data.melt1, site ~ survey)
sample.matrix[sample.matrix==0] <- NA

data.melt2 <- melt(data, id.var=c("site","survey"), measure.var="count")
count.matrix <- cast(data.melt2, site ~ survey)

count.matrix <- count.matrix*sample.matrix

hi Alex et al,

one general comment on your PS at the bottom: one of the many practical things of a Bayesian MCMC-based analysis is that you can do a sequential analysis. For instance, if you have a large data set and analyse it using some model, then you get exactly the same answer (i.e., param estimates) in principle as when you, say, cut the data set into three subsets and then work through them one at a time, using the posterior from one as a prior for the next. Hence, if you analyse one part of your data and then use the estimates from that analysis as an informative prior in the next analysis, then it's exactly as conducting an "integrated" analysis of the entire data set in the first place.

There are a couple of caveats, for instance, it is trivial in practice to take the posterior mean and standard deviation of a parameter at one step and then specify a Normal prior with those parameters as a prior in the next. However, this assumes that the posterior is symmetric and the info in the posterior is summarised well by the mean and sd of a normal. Of course, for a variance or a standard deviation param, which typically have skewed posteriors, you could take the log. Further, it also assumed that there is no estimation covariance between two or more parameters. If there is, then you might have to specify a multivariate normal prior for the params.

Doing statistics on statistics (two-step analyses) has had a bit a bad reputation, at least since Bill Link's 1999 paper in JWM, but sometimes it makes things much easier. There is also a recent paper by Murtaugh in Ecology who argues that sometimes doing a hierarchical "by hand" in this way may be more practical than doing it all at once. What is sure is that with a Bayesian analysis, error propagation is much easier than with a likelihood analysis. So, I think that we should not a priori discard the possibility to conduct an analysis in two steps instead of analysing a complicated data set all at once.

Kind regards  --  Marc

On Sat, Nov 23, 2013 at 12:14 AM, Dan Linden <danl...@gmail.com> wrote:

> I don't see a problem with using the effective strip width.  Granted, it's an ad hoc adjustment that does not account for all uncertainty as you could with a more complex model (MRDS?) but that route might be more complicated than you need here, especially if the subset is small.
>
> In this scenario pcount would then be modeling availability, not detectability.  The distance sampling adjustment has taken care of detectability, so changes in counts across surveys indicates individuals that were not available to be detected during certain surveys.
